title: Experimental VLE, consistency and fitting
narration: Welcome to Session Two. This independent lesson is about experimental vapor-liquid equilibrium, consistency, and model fitting. We will begin with the ideal-mixture ideas from our first lesson, then introduce the activity coefficient step by step. You do not need to know what gamma means before starting. Allow about three hours for the whole lesson, including your calculations, the Lab investigation, and the review questions. The narration is only part of that time. When asked to pause, stop the recording and do the activity before continuing.
pause_instruction: Advance to the schedule. No calculation or worksheet entry is required on the title slide.

title: A three-hour independent lesson
narration: This lesson replaces the class on the sixteenth of October. Read the schedule as a guide to your total working time. The first ten minutes are for preparation. Then we spend twenty-five minutes checking phases and material balances. Next, we introduce liquid nonideality, followed by a separate Antoine equation exercise. After a ten-minute break, you will investigate a dataset in Lab Eight. The final thirty-five minutes are for the review test, corrections, the exit ticket, and feedback. The times shown on later slides are elapsed lesson time, not the length of the audio. A short explanation may be followed by several minutes of your own work. Pause before every solution and use the remaining time in each section to calculate and check your reasoning.
pause_instruction: Read the schedule, then advance. The 180 minutes include independent work and the break.

title: Preparation · 0–10 min
narration: First, download the four-page worksheet using the link on this slide. Keep the worksheet and this slide deck open side by side, or print the worksheet if you prefer. Have a calculator and some extra paper ready. Do not start the exercises yet, and you do not need to open the Lab until minute one hundred. The three-page reading is optional background. All the instructions needed for today's activities are in this deck. Our first lesson used ideal-mixture vapor-liquid equilibrium. Today we will ask what happens when a liquid mixture does not follow that ideal prediction. By the end, you should be able to calculate an activity coefficient from one observation, check the conventions behind an Antoine equation, and interpret a comparison between two fitted models. Take the rest of this preparation period to get your materials ready.
pause_instruction: Open worksheet pages 1–4, prepare a calculator and paper, and resume with the composition review at about minute 10. Do not open the Lab yet.

title: 1. Composition and phase amount · 10–15 min
narration: Before introducing anything new, let us separate composition from phase amount. The symbol z means the overall mole fraction in the feed. The symbol x means the mole fraction within the liquid phase, and y means the mole fraction within the vapor phase. Beta is different: it is the fraction of the total moles that are in the vapor. For component one, the material balance says: z one equals the quantity one minus beta, multiplied by x one, plus beta multiplied by y one. The two terms are the liquid and vapor contributions to the overall composition. Also check composition sums separately. All the x values in an existing liquid phase must add to one, and all the y values in an existing vapor phase must add to one. Read this slide carefully. No worksheet answer is needed yet; Section A begins on the next slide.
pause_instruction: Read the symbol definitions and material balance on this slide. No worksheet entry is required. Advance when ready for A1–A3.

title: Pause and calculate · 15–23 min
narration: Now open page one of the worksheet and complete A one through A three. Use the ideal binary mixture and saturation pressures given here. First calculate the bubble pressure using the weighted sum. Then calculate the dew pressure by taking the reciprocal of the sum shown in the second equation. Keep the pressures in kilopascals. Use those two boundaries to classify the states at eighty, ninety-five, and one hundred ten kilopascals. Finally, at one hundred ten kilopascals, report beta and x one, and explain whether a vapor composition exists. Show your substitutions. No Lab is needed. Pause the recording now and finish A one through A three before viewing the solution.
pause_instruction: Pause and complete worksheet page 1, A1–A3, with a calculator. Resume at the phase-check slide after attempting all three items.

At eighty kilopascals, the mixture is vapor. At ninety-five, it contains liquid and vapor. At one hundred ten, it is liquid. In that last case, beta is zero and x one equals the overall composition, zero point five. There is no vapor phase, so there is no vapor composition to report. title: Material-balance check · 32–35 min
narration: Your two contributions should be approximately zero point one nine six nine seven and zero point three zero three zero three. Together, they give z one equal to zero point five, allowing for rounding in the supplied values. The other liquid composition, x two, is zero point six one one one one one. The other vapor composition, y two, is zero point three eight five nine six five. Each phase sum is one. These are simple but useful checks: a convincing graph does not guarantee that values have been copied correctly. Keep the substituted balance in A four and correct any mismatch before moving on.

title: 2. Starting from Raoult’s law · 35–39 min
narration: We will now build from the ideal-liquid model you already know. With an ideal liquid mixture and ideal vapor, Raoult's law says: y i times total pressure equals x i times the pure component's saturation pressure at the same temperature. The left side is the component's vapor partial pressure. Consider component one. Its liquid mole fraction is zero point four, and its saturation pressure is one hundred twenty kilopascals. The ideal prediction is therefore forty-eight kilopascals. Now suppose an observation gives a vapor mole fraction of zero point six at a total pressure of one hundred kilopascals. Its partial pressure is sixty kilopascals. We have a gap between observation and prediction. On scratch paper, calculate sixty divided by forty-eight. What multiplying factor would make the ideal prediction match this observation? You do not need a new worksheet entry yet.
pause_instruction: On scratch paper, calculate 60 divided by 48. Think about what this ratio compares, then advance.

title: A new quantity: activity coefficient · 39–42 min
narration: The ratio is one point two five. We call this multiplying factor the activity coefficient, pronounced gamma. This is a new quantity for today's lesson. In the modified Raoult equation, we multiply the liquid mole fraction by gamma and by the saturation pressure. Gamma equal to one gives back the ideal-liquid prediction. A value above one gives a higher partial pressure than that prediction, while a value below one gives a lower partial pressure, under the same assumptions. For our example, multiplying forty-eight kilopascals by one point two five gives the observed sixty kilopascals. We are still assuming an ideal vapor and neglecting the Poynting correction, which accounts for pressure effects on the liquid reference state. Before interpreting gamma as liquid nonideality, check the observations and the saturation-pressure input. An incorrect property input can also change the gamma value inferred from the data.
pause_instruction: Compare gamma = 1.25 with your scratch calculation. Read the assumptions, then advance; no Lab or worksheet entry is required.

title: Activity and its reference · 42–45 min
narration: We can now define activity. In the convention used here, activity equals gamma times the liquid mole fraction. It represents composition adjusted for nonideal behavior, with the pure liquid as the reference state. Both activity and the activity coefficient are dimensionless. For an ideal liquid solution, gamma equals one, so activity is simply the mole fraction. In our example, gamma one is one point two five and x one is zero point four. Their product is an activity of zero point five zero. Notice that the composition has not changed: x one is still zero point four. Activity is a thermodynamic quantity derived from that composition and gamma; it is not a new mole fraction. Check this multiplication on your calculator, but leave worksheet Section B blank until the calculation exercise begins.
pause_instruction: Check 1.25 times 0.4 on your calculator. Read the reference-state statement and keep worksheet B blank until the exercise at minute 48.

title: Calculating gamma from VLE · 45–48 min
narration: To estimate gamma from an equilibrium observation, rearrange the modified Raoult equation. Gamma i equals y i times total pressure, divided by the product of x i and the saturation pressure. Read the denominator as one complete product: liquid mole fraction times saturation pressure. The numerator and denominator must use the same pressure units, so those units cancel. The result is dimensionless. We also need the saturation pressure at the observation's temperature, not at some other temperature. This calculation assumes ideal vapor and a negligible Poynting correction. It gives an inferred gamma under those assumptions and with the chosen property correlation. It does not independently prove that all those inputs are correct. Keep this equation available. On the next slide, you will use it in B one through B three on worksheet page one.
pause_instruction: Read the rearranged equation and its assumptions. Have worksheet page 1, B1–B3 ready for the next slide.

title: Pause: one observation, two property inputs · 48–57 min
narration: Complete B one through B three on worksheet page one. Use the synthetic observation on this slide: total pressure one hundred kilopascals, x one zero point four, and y one zero point six. In B one, use a saturation pressure of one hundred twenty kilopascals to calculate gamma one and activity one. In B two, repeat with one hundred fifty kilopascals. For B three, explain what changed and whether the observed mixture data changed. Then consider whether fitting alone could establish which saturation-pressure input is correct. Show substitution and pressure-unit cancellation. Pause now, and finish your own calculations and explanation before viewing the answer.
pause_instruction: Pause and complete worksheet page 1, B1–B3. Use only the observation on this slide; no Lab is needed.

title: A property error changes inferred activity · 57–65 min
narration: With a saturation pressure of one hundred twenty kilopascals, gamma one is one point two five and activity one is zero point five zero. With one hundred fifty kilopascals, gamma one becomes one, and activity one becomes zero point four zero. The measured pressure and both observed compositions stayed the same. Only the assumed pure-component saturation pressure changed. Because that property appears in the denominator, increasing it lowers the inferred gamma. A fitted model may compensate for a property error by changing its parameters. A small fitting error therefore does not tell us which property input is correct. Compare the table with B one and B two, then finish B three with a sentence explaining why the property source needs an independent check. Keep your original work and add corrections beside it.
pause_instruction: Check worksheet page 1, B1–B3, correct the calculations, and finish the explanation in B3 before continuing to Antoine conventions.

title: 3. Antoine conventions · 65–72 min
narration: We now need to calculate saturation pressure as temperature changes. The Antoine equation provides a correlation, but its constants only make sense with the convention stated by their source. In the form shown here, take log base ten of saturation pressure divided by the specified pressure unit. The right side is A minus B divided by the quantity temperature plus C. Check the exact equation, the logarithm base, and the sign used with C. Then check the temperature unit and the pressure unit. Finally, check the component identity and the valid temperature range. These details are part of the property model. Selecting a different unit or logarithm in a menu does not automatically convert the constants you have entered. Open page two of the worksheet and locate Section C. Read these checks before advancing. Leave Section D blank for now; that section belongs to the later Lab activity.
pause_instruction: Pause to read the Antoine convention checks and locate Section C on worksheet page 2. Do not start Section D. Continue at minute 72.

First, calculate saturation pressure at fifty degrees Celsius. Show your substitution and the step that converts the logarithm back into pressure. Then explain the temperature-unit issue, the change of logarithm base, and the validity-range issue. Use only the correlation on this slide. Do not enter these teaching constants into Lab Eight. Pause the narration and work through all four questions. Keep your original answers so that you can compare them with the solution on the next slide.
pause_instruction: Pause and complete worksheet page 2, C1–C4. Show substitutions. Do not open the solution until you have attempted all four questions. Continue at minute 82.

title: Antoine check · 82–90 min
narration: Check C one through C four on page two. At fifty degrees Celsius, the denominator is fifty plus two hundred. Four minus one thousand divided by two hundred and fifty is zero. Therefore, saturation pressure is ten to the power zero kilopascals, or one kilopascal. The temperature variable requires Celsius, so first convert three hundred twenty-three point one five kelvin to fifty degrees Celsius. Changing from log base ten to natural logarithm requires corresponding constants. At this particular point, however, the exponent is zero, so both bases happen to give one. This single point cannot reveal that mistake. Finally, one hundred degrees Celsius is outside the stated range. Add corrections and reasons beside your original answers.
pause_instruction: Pause to correct worksheet page 2, C1–C4 and explain any errors. Begin the break at minute 90.

title: Interpreting the comparison · 135–145 min
narration: Before choosing a conclusion, separate four kinds of evidence. Solver convergence tells us that an optimizer met its stopping criterion. Small training residuals tell us how closely the model reproduces the observations used for fitting. A thermodynamic consistency diagnostic asks whether data agree with a thermodynamic constraint under the diagnostic's stated assumptions. Prediction requires a different check, using observations that were excluded from fitting. These are different questions. In this example, the synthetic data were generated with N R T L. A close N R T L fit is therefore expected model recovery, not evidence that it is universally the best model. Now complete Section F on worksheet page three. Use your E two results to write one finding, support it with numerical evidence and units, and state one limitation. No additional Lab or dataset is required for this step. Pause here to finish Section F, then continue to the review test.

title: Review solutions · 165–169 min
